original_value: Identifying people in historical photographs is important for preserving material culture, correcting the historical record, and creating economic value, but it is also a complex and challenging task. In this article, we focus on identifying portraits of soldiers who participated in the American Civil War (1861--65), the first widely photographed conflict. Many thousands of these portraits survive, but only 10%--20% are identified. We created Photo Sleuth, a web-based platform that combines crowdsourced human expertise and automated face recognition to support Civil War portrait identification. Our mixed-methods evaluations of Photo Sleuth one month and 11 months after its public launch showed that it helped users successfully identify unknown portraits and provided a sustainable model for volunteer contribution. We also discuss implications for crowd-AI interaction and person identification pipelines.

result.paraphrase: Identifying people in historical photographs is vital for preserving material culture, correcting the historical record, and generating economic value, though it is a difficult and complex task. In this article, we examine portraits of soldiers who took part in the American Civil War (1861--65), the first widely photographed conflict. Tens of thousands of these portraits still exist, yet only 10%--20% have been identified. To aid Civil War portrait identification, we built Photo Sleuth, a web-based platform that merges crowdsourced human expertise with automated face recognition. Mixed-methods evaluations conducted one month and 11 months after Photo Sleuth’s public launch found that it helped users identify unknown portraits successfully and offered a sustainable model for volunteer contribution. We also consider the implications for crowd-AI interaction and person-identification pipelines.
